nodes.name: No unobserved selection variables
nodes.statement:
However, in this paper we assume that there are no
unobserved selection variables.

nodes.name: Graph
nodes.statement: A graph $\g= (\vars,\e) $ consists of a set of nodes (variables) $ \vars=\left\lbrace X_{1},\dots,X_{p}\right\rbrace$ and a set of edges $ \e $.
nodes.statement_short: A graph G=(V,E) is a node set V with an edge set E.

nodes.name: Adjacent nodes
nodes.statement: There is at most one edge between any pair of nodes, and nodes are called \textit{adjacent} if they are connected by an edge.

nodes.name: Edge marks
nodes.statement: Every edge has two edge marks that can be arrowheads, tails or circles.

nodes.name: Edge types (directed, bidirected, non-directed, partially directed)
nodes.statement: Edges can be \emph{directed} $\rightarrow$,  \emph{bidirected}  $\leftrightarrow$, \emph{non-directed} $\setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture}$ or \emph{partially directed} $\setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.2,0){$\rightarrow$} \end{picture}$.

nodes.name: Edge-mark wildcard $\bullet$
nodes.statement: We use $\bullet$ as a stand in for any of the allowed edge marks.

nodes.name: Edge into / out of a node
nodes.statement: An edge is \textit{into} (\textit{out of}) a node $X$ if the edge has an arrowhead (tail) at $X$.

nodes.name: Directed graph
nodes.statement: A \emph{directed graph} contains only directed edges.

nodes.name: Mixed graph
nodes.statement: A \emph{mixed graph} may contain directed and bi-directed edges.

nodes.name: Path
nodes.statement: A \textit{path} $p$ from $X$ to $Y$ in $\g$ is a sequence of distinct nodes $\langle X, \dots,Y \rangle$ in which every pair of successive nodes is adjacent in $\g$.
differentia: every pair of successive nodes is adjacent in $\g$

nodes.name: Node lies on a path
nodes.statement: A node $V$ \emph{lies on a path} $p$ if $V$ occurs in the sequence of nodes.

nodes.name: Length of a path
nodes.statement: The \textit{length} of a path equals the number of edges on the path.

nodes.name: Directed path
nodes.statement: A \textit{directed path} from $X$ to $Y$ is a path from $X$ to $Y$ in which all edges are directed towards $Y$, i.e., $X \to \dots\to Y$.

nodes.name: Causal path
nodes.statement: A directed path is also called a \textit{causal path}.

nodes.name: Possibly directed (possibly causal) path
nodes.statement: A \textit{possibly directed path} (\textit{possibly causal path}) from $X$ to $Y$ is a path from $X$ to $Y$ that has no arrowhead pointing to $X$.

nodes.name: Non-causal path
nodes.statement: A path from $X$ to $Y$ that is not possibly causal is called a \textit{non-causal path} from $X$ to $Y$.

nodes.name: (Almost) directed cycle
nodes.statement: A directed path from $X$ to $Y$ together with an edge $Y\to X$ ($Y \leftrightarrow X$) forms an \emph{(almost) directed cycle}.

nodes.name: Path between node sets
nodes.statement:
For two disjoint subsets $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ of $\mathbf{V}$, a path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$
is a path from some $X \in \mathbf{X}$ to some $Y \in \mathbf{Y}$.

nodes.name: Proper path
nodes.statement: A path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ is \textit{proper} if only its first node is in $\mathbf{X}$.

nodes.name: Subsequence of a path
nodes.statement: A \textit{subsequence} of a path $p$ is a sequence of nodes obtained by deleting some nodes from $p$ without changing the order of the remaining nodes.

nodes.name: Subpath
nodes.statement: For a path $p = \langle X_1,X_2,\dots,X_m \rangle$, the \textit{subpath} from $X_i$ to $X_k$ ($1\le i\le k\le m)$ is the path $p(X_i,X_k) = \langle X_i,X_{i+1},\dots,X_{k}\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: The subpath p(X_i,X_k) of a path p is the stretch of p between X_i and X_k.

nodes.name: Path concatenation $\oplus$
nodes.statement:
We denote the concatenation of paths by $\oplus$, so
that for example $p = p(X_1,X_{k}) \oplus p(X_{k},X_{m})$.

nodes.name: Parent
nodes.statement: If $X\to Y$, then $X$ is a \textit{parent} of $Y$.

nodes.name: (Possible) ancestor and descendant
nodes.statement: If there is a (possibly) directed path from $X$ to $Y$, then $X$ is a \textit{(possible) ancestor} of $Y$, and $Y$ is a \textit{(possible) descendant} of $X$.

nodes.name: Notation Pa and (Poss)De
nodes.statement: The sets of parents and (possible) descendants of $X$ in $\g$ are denoted by $\mathrm{Pa}(X,\g)$ and $(Poss)De(X,\g)$ respectively.

nodes.name: Pa and (Poss)De of a set
nodes.statement: For a set of nodes $\mathbf{X} \subseteq \mathbf{V}$, we have $\mathrm{Pa}(\mathbf{X},\g) = \cup_{X \in \mathbf{X}} \mathrm{Pa}(X,\g)$, with analogous definitions for $(Poss)De(\mathbf{X},\g)$.

nodes.name: Collider
nodes.statement: If a path $p$ contains $X_i \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(0.2,0){$\bullet$} \put(1,0){$\rightarrow$} \end{picture} X_j \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(0.2,0){$\leftarrow$} \put(3,0){$\bullet$} \end{picture} X_k$ as a subpath, then $X_j$ is a \textit{collider} on $p$.

nodes.name: Collider path
nodes.statement: A \textit{collider path} is a path on which every non-endpoint node is a collider.

nodes.name: (Un)shielded triple
nodes.statement: A path $\langle X_{i},X_{j},X_{k} \rangle$ is an \emph{(un)shielded triple} if $ X_{i} $ and $ X_{k}$ are (not) adjacent.

nodes.name: Unshielded path
nodes.statement: A path is \textit{unshielded} if all successive triples on the path are unshielded.

nodes.name: Definite non-collider
nodes.statement: A node $X_{j}$ is a \textit{definite non-collider} on a path $p$ if there is at least one edge out of $X_{j}$ on $p$, or if $X_{i} \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(0.2,0){$\bullet$} \put(1.1, 1){\line(1,0){2.4}} \put(4, 1){\circle{1}} \end{picture} X_j \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2.4}} \put(2.9,0){$\bullet$} \end{picture} X_k$ is a subpath of $p$ and $\langle X_i,X_j,X_k\rangle$ is an unshielded triple.
nodes.statement_short: X_j is a definite non-collider on p if p has an edge out of X_j, or X_j sits as a circle-circle middle of an unshielded triple.

nodes.name: Definite status node
nodes.statement: A node is of \textit{definite status} on a path if it is a collider or a definite non-collider on the path.

nodes.name: Definite status path
nodes.statement: A path $p$ is of definite status if every non-endpoint node on $p$ is of definite status.

nodes.name: Unshielded paths are of definite status
nodes.statement:
An unshielded path is always of definite status, but a
definite status path is not always unshielded.
conclusions: An unshielded path is always of definite status
definite status path is not always unshielded

nodes.name: m-connecting path
nodes.statement: A definite status path \textit{p} between nodes $X$ and $Y$ is \textit{m-connecting} given a set of nodes $\mathbf{Z}$ ($X,Y \notin \mathbf{Z}$) if every definite non-collider on $p$ is not in $\mathbf{Z}$, and every collider on $p$ has a descendant in $\mathbf{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: A definite status path is m-connecting given Z if no definite non-collider is in Z and every collider has a descendant in Z.

nodes.name: Blocked path
nodes.statement: Otherwise $\mathbf{Z}$ blocks $p$.

nodes.name: m-separation
nodes.statement: If $\mathbf{Z}$ blocks all definite status paths between $X$ and $Y$, we say that $X$ and $Y$ are m-separated given $\mathbf{Z}$.

nodes.name: m-connected nodes
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $X$ and $Y$ are m-connected given $\mathbf{Z}$.

nodes.name: m-separation of sets
nodes.statement: For pairwise disjoint subsets $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ of $\vars$, $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{Y}$ are m-separated given $\mathbf{Z}$ if $X$ and $Y$ are m-separated by $\mathbf{Z}$ for any $X \in \mathbf{X}$ and $Y\in \mathbf{Y}$.

nodes.name: Directed acyclic graph (DAG)
nodes.statement: A directed graph without directed cycles is a \emph{directed acyclic graph ($\mathrm{DAG})$}.

nodes.name: Bayesian network
nodes.statement: A Bayesian network for a set of variables $\vars=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{p}\}$ is a pair ($\g,f$), where $\g$ is a $\mathrm{DAG}$, and $f$ is a joint probability density for $\vars$ that factorizes according to the conditional independence relationships described via m-separation, that is $f(\vars)= \prod_{i=1}^{p}f(X_{i}|Pa(X_{i},\g))$ \citep{Pearl2009}.
nodes.statement_short: A Bayesian network is a DAG with a joint density factorizing as the product of conditionals given parents.

nodes.name: Causal DAG
nodes.statement: We call a $\mathrm{DAG}$ causal when every edge $X_{i} \rightarrow X_{j}$ in $\g$ represents a direct causal effect of $X_{i}$ on $X_{j}$.

nodes.name: Causal Bayesian network
nodes.statement: A Bayesian network ($\g,f$) is a \emph{causal Bayesian network} if $\g$ is a causal $\mathrm{DAG}$.

nodes.name: Intervention do(X=x) and post-intervention density
nodes.statement_short: Interventions do(X=x) set X to x; the post-intervention density is the truncated product of conditionals of the non-intervened variables.

nodes.name: Truncated factorization formula (g-formula)
nodes.statement_short: Post-intervention density: product of the conditionals of non-intervened variables given parents, zero if inconsistent with x.

nodes.name: Ancestral graph
nodes.statement: A mixed graph $\g$ without directed cycles and almost directed cycles is called \textit{ancestral}.
differentia: without directed cycles and almost directed cycles

nodes.name: Maximal ancestral graph (MAG)
nodes.statement: A \emph{maximal ancestral graph ($\mathrm{MAG}$)} is an ancestral graph $\g = (\vars, \e)$ where every two non-adjacent nodes $X$ and $Y$ in $\g$ can be m-separated by a set $\mathbf{Z} \subseteq \vars \setminus \{X,Y\}$.
differentia: every two non-adjacent nodes $X$ and $Y$ in $\g$ can be m-separated by a set $\mathbf{Z} \subseteq \vars \setminus \{X,Y\}$

nodes.name: MAG representation of DAGs with latent variables
nodes.statement: A $\mathrm{DAG}$ with unobserved variables can be uniquely represented by a $\mathrm{MAG}$ that preserves the ancestral and m-separation relationships among the observed variables \citep{richardson2002ancestral}.
assumptions: A $\mathrm{DAG}$ with unobserved variables
conclusions: can be uniquely represented by a $\mathrm{MAG}$ that preserves the ancestral and m-separation relationships among the observed variables

nodes.name: Causal MAG
nodes.statement: The $\mathrm{MAG}$ of a causal $\mathrm{DAG}$ is a \emph{causal $\mathrm{MAG}$}.

nodes.name: Markov equivalence class and CPDAG
nodes.statement: Several $\mathrm{DAG}$s can encode the same conditional independence information via m-separation. Such $\mathrm{DAG}$s form a \emph{Markov equivalence class} which can be described uniquely by a \emph{completed partially directed acyclic graph ($\mathrm{CPDAG}$)} .

nodes.name: Partial ancestral graph (PAG)
nodes.statement: Several $\mathrm{MAG}$s can also encode the same conditional independence information. Such $\mathrm{MAG}$s form a Markov equivalence class which can be described uniquely by a \emph{partial ancestral graph ($\mathrm{PAG}$)} \citep{richardson2002ancestral, ali2009markov}.

nodes.name: Equivalence class notation $[\g]$
nodes.statement: We denote all $\mathrm{DAG}$s ($\mathrm{MAG}$s) in the Markov equivalence class described by a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ by $[\g]$.

nodes.name: Density consistent with a causal DAG
nodes.statement: A density $f$ is \textit{consistent} with a causal $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$ if the pair ($\g[D],f$) forms a causal Bayesian network.

nodes.name: Density consistent with a causal MAG
nodes.statement: A density $f$ is consistent with a causal $\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$ if there exists a causal Bayesian network ($\g[D]',f'$), such that $\g[M]$ represents $\g[D]'$ and $f$ is the observed marginal of $f'$.

nodes.name: Density consistent with a CPDAG (PAG)
nodes.statement: A density $f$ is consistent with a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ if it is consistent with a $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$.

nodes.name: Visible edges in DAGs and CPDAGs
nodes.statement: All directed edges in $\mathrm{DAG}$s and $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s are said to be visible.

nodes.name: Visible edge (MAG/PAG)
nodes.statement: Given a $\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$ or a $\mathrm{PAG}$ $\g$, a directed edge $X \rightarrow Y$ is \textit{visible} if there is a node $V$ not adjacent to $Y$ such that there is an edge between $V$ and $X$ that is into $X$, or if there is a collider path from $V$ to $X$ that is into $X$ and every non-endpoint node on the path is a parent of $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: In a MAG/PAG, X->Y is visible if some V not adjacent to Y has an edge into X, or a collider path into X through parents of Y.

nodes.name: Invisible edge
nodes.statement: Otherwise, $X \rightarrow Y$ is said to be \textit{invisible} \citep{zhang2006causal, maathuis2013generalized}.

nodes.name: Visible edges exclude latent confounding
nodes.statement: A directed visible edge $X\rightarrow Y$ means that there are no latent confounders between $X$ and $Y$.

nodes.name: Setting: graph and disjoint node sets X, Y, Z
nodes.statement: Throughout, let $\g=(\vars,\e)$ represent a $\mathrm{DAG}$, $\mathrm{CPDAG}$, $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$, and let $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ be pairwise disjoint subsets of $\vars$, with $\mathbf{X}\neq \emptyset$ and $\mathbf{Y}\neq \emptyset$.

nodes.name: Intervention and response variables
nodes.statement: Here $\mathbf{X}$ represents the intervention variables and $\mathbf{Y}$ represents the set of response variables, i.e., we are interested in the causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$.

nodes.name: Adjustment set
nodes.statement_short: Z is an adjustment set for (X,Y) if for every density consistent with G, f(y|do(x)) equals the Z-adjusted conditional of y given x.
nodes.label: defadjustment

nodes.name: Adjustment amenability
nodes.statement:
{(\textbf{Amenability for $DAG$s, $CPDAG$s, $MAG$s and $PAG$s})}
  A $\mathrm{DAG}$, $\mathrm{CPDAG}$, $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$ $\g$ is said to be adjustment amenable, relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ if every possibly directed proper path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ in $\g$ starts with a visible edge out of $\mathbf{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: G is amenable w.r.t. (X,Y) if every possibly directed proper path from X to Y starts with a visible edge out of X.
nodes.label: defadjamengen

nodes.name: Amenable (shorthand)
nodes.statement: For conciseness, we will also write ``amenable'' instead of ``adjustment amenable''.

nodes.name: Intuition behind amenability
nodes.statement_short: In MAGs/PAGs a directed edge may mix causation and latent confounding, and CPDAG/PAG edges may be undirected, so a path can be causal in some represented DAGs but not others.

nodes.name: Every DAG is amenable
nodes.statement: Note that every $\mathrm{DAG}$ is amenable, since all edges in a $\mathrm{DAG}$ are visible and directed.

nodes.name: Amenability for MAGs coincides with van der Zander et al.
nodes.statement: For $\mathrm{MAG}$s, our notion of amenability reduces to the one defined by \citet{vanconstructing}.

nodes.name: Generalized Adjustment Criterion (GAC)
differentia: no element in $\mathbf{Z}$ is a possible descendant in $\g$ of any $W \in \vars\setminus\mathbf{X}$ which lies on a proper possibly causal path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$
all proper definite status non-causal paths in $\g$ from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ are blocked by $\mathbf{Z}$
nodes.statement_short: Z satisfies the GAC if G is amenable, Z has no possible descendant of a non-X node on a proper possibly causal path, and Z blocks all proper definite status non-causal paths.
nodes.label: defacgen

nodes.name: Condition (0) does not depend on Z
nodes.statement: Note that condition (0) does not depend on $\mathbf{Z}$. In other words, if condition (0) is violated, then there is no set $\mathbf{Z'} \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup\mathbf{Y})$ that satisfies the generalized adjustment criterion relative to $(\mathbf{X,Y})$ in $\g$.

nodes.name: Forbidden nodes $\mathbf{F}_{\g}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$
nodes.statement:
Condition (1) defines a set of nodes that cannot be used in an adjustment set. Denoting this set of forbidden nodes by
\begin{align} \fb{\g} = \{ & W' \in \vars: W' \in \mathrm{PossDe}(W,\g) \,\text{for some} \notag \\
   &  W \notin \mathbf{X} \,\text{which lies on a proper possibly} \notag \\
   &  \text{causal path from} \, \mathbf{X} \,\text{to}\, \mathbf{Y}\},
\end{align}
condition (1) can be stated as: $\mathbf{Z} \cap \fb{\g} = \emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: The forbidden set F_G(X,Y) is all possible descendants of non-X nodes on proper possibly causal X-Y paths; condition (1) says Z avoids it.

nodes.name: Forbidden node set (2)
nodes.label: eq: def forbidden nodes

nodes.name: Generalized adjustment criterion is sound and complete
nodes.statement: Let $\g$ represent a $\mathrm{DAG}$, $\mathrm{CPDAG}$, $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$. Then $\mathbf{Z}$ is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (Definition \ref{defadjustment}) if and only if $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies the generalized adjustment criterion  relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (Definition \ref{defacgen}).
assumptions: Let $\g$ represent a $\mathrm{DAG}$, $\mathrm{CPDAG}$, $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$.
conclusions: $\mathbf{Z}$ is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (Definition \ref{defadjustment}) if and only if $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies the generalized adjustment criterion  relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (Definition \ref{defacgen})
equivalent_conditions: $\mathbf{Z}$ is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (Definition \ref{defadjustment})
$\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies the generalized adjustment criterion  relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (Definition \ref{defacgen})
nodes.statement_short: For DAGs, CPDAGs, MAGs and PAGs, Z is a valid adjustment set for (X,Y) iff Z satisfies the generalized adjustment criterion.
nodes.label: thmgenac

nodes.name: Adjustment sets in a CPDAG (introduction example)
nodes.statement: We first return to the example of the Introduction. Consider the $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ $\g[C]$ in Figure~\ref{fig:cpdagexample}a. Note that $\g[C]$ is amenable relative to ($X,Y$) and that $\f{\g[C]} = \{ Y \}$. Hence, any node other than $X$ and $Y$ can be used in an adjustment set. Note that every definite status non-causal path $p$ from $X$ to $Y$ has one of the following paths as a subsequence: $p_1 = \langle X, Z,Y\rangle$ and $p_2 = \langle X, A,B, Y\rangle$, and nodes on $p$ that are not on $p_1$ or $p_2$ are non-colliders on $p$. Hence, if we block $p_1$ and $p_2$, then we block all definite status non-causal paths from $X$ to $Y$. This implies that any superset of $\{Z,A\}$ and $\{Z,B\}$ is an adjustment set relative to $(X,Y)$ in $\g[C]$, and all adjustment sets are given by: $\{Z,A\}$, $\{Z,B\},\{Z,A,I\},\{Z,B,I\},\{Z,A,B\}$ and $\{Z,A,B,I\}$.
nodes.statement_short: In the CPDAG of Figure 1a, the forbidden set is {Y} and the adjustment sets are the supersets of {Z,A} or {Z,B} avoiding X,Y.
nodes.label: ex1

nodes.name: Amenability in a PAG and two MAGs
nodes.statement:
To illustrate the concept of amenability, consider Figure~\ref{figex2} with a $\mathrm{PAG}$ $\g[P]$ in (a), and two $\mathrm{MAG}$s $\g[M]_1$ and $\g[M]_2$ in $[\g[P]]$ in (b) and (c). Note that $\g[P]$ and $\g[M]_1$ are not amenable relative to $(X,Y)$. For $\g[P]$ this is due to the path $X \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture} Y$, and for $\g[M]_1$ this is due to the invisible edge $X \to Y$. On the other hand, $\g[M]_2$ is amenable relative to $(X,Y)$, since the edges $X\to Y$ and $X \to V_2$ are visible due to the edge $V_1\to X$ and the fact that $V_1$ is not adjacent to $Y$ or $V_2$.
   Since there are no proper definite status non-causal paths from $X$ to $Y$ in $\g[M]_2$, it follows that the empty set satisfies the generalized adjustment criterion relative to $(X,Y)$ in $\g[M]_2$.
   Finally, note that $\g[M]_1$ could also be interpreted as a $\mathrm{DAG}$. In that case it would be amenable relative to $(X,Y)$. This shows that amenability depends crucially on the interpretation of the graph.
nodes.statement_short: A PAG and one MAG in its class are not amenable while another MAG is; amenability depends on interpreting the graph as DAG or MAG.
nodes.label: ex2

nodes.name: Amenability is not sufficient for adjustment
nodes.statement:
Let $\g[P]_1$ and $\g[P]_2$ be the $\mathrm{PAG}$s in Figure~\ref{figex3}(a) and Figure~\ref{figex3}(b), respectively.
  Both $\mathrm{PAG}$s are amenable relative to $(X,Y)$. We will show that there is an adjustment set relative to $(X,Y)$ in $\g[P]_1$ but not in $\g[P]_2$. This illustrates that amenability is not a sufficient
  criterion for the existence of an adjustment set.

  We first consider $\g[P]_1$. Note that  $\f{\g[P]_1} = \{ V_4, Y \}$ is the set of nodes that cannot be used for adjustment.  There are two proper definite status non-causal paths from $X$ to $Y$ in $\g[P]_1$: $X \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(0.2,0){$\leftarrow$} \put(4.3,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture} V_3 \rightarrow Y$ and $X \rightarrow V_4 \leftarrow V_3 \rightarrow Y$. These are blocked by any set containing $V_3$. Hence, all sets satisfying the GAC relative to ($X,Y$) in $\g[P]_1$ are: $\{ V_3 \}$, $\{V_1, V_3 \}, \{V_2, V_3 \}$ and $\{ V_1, V_2, V_3 \}$.

  We now consider $\g[P]_2$. Note that $\f{\g[P]_2} = \f{\g[P]_1} = \{ V_4, Y \}$. There are three proper definite status non-causal paths from $X$ to $Y$ in $\g[P]_2$:  $p_1 = X \leftrightarrow V_3 \rightarrow Y$, $p_2 = X \leftrightarrow V_3 \leftrightarrow V_4 \to Y$ and  $p_3 = X \rightarrow V_4 \leftrightarrow V_3 \rightarrow Y$. To block $p_1$, we must also use $V_3$. This implies that we must use $V_4$ to block $p_2$. But $V_4 \in \f{\g[P]_2}$. Hence, there is no set $\mathbf{Z}$ that satisfies the GAC relative to ($X,Y$) in $\g[P]_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Two amenable PAGs, one with adjustment sets and one without: amenability does not guarantee an adjustment set exists.
nodes.label: ex3

nodes.name: GAC versus generalized back-door criterion
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{X} = \{X_1,X_2\}$ and $\mathbf{Y} = \{Y\}$ and consider the $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ $\g[C]$ and the $\mathrm{PAG}$ $\g[P]$ in Figures \ref{figex4}(a) and \ref{figex4}(b). We will show that for both graphs there is no set that satisfies the generalized back-door criterion of  \cite{maathuis2013generalized} relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$, but there are sets that satisfy the generalized adjustment criterion relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in these graphs.
  
   Recall that a set $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies the generalized back-door criterion relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ and a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ if $\mathbf{Z}$ contains no possible descendants of $\mathbf{X}$ in $\g$ and if for every $X \in \mathbf{X}$ the set $\mathbf{Z}\cup \mathbf{X}\setminus\{X\}$ blocks every definite status path from $X$ to every $Y \in \mathbf{Y}$ in $\g$ that does not start with a visible edge out of $X$.

   We first consider the $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ $\g[C]$. 
   To block the path $X_2 \leftarrow V_2 \leftarrow Y$, we must use node $V_2$, but $V_2 \in \mathrm{PossDe}(X_1, \g[C])$. Hence, no set $\mathbf{Z}$ can satisfy the generalized back-door criterion relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[C]$. However, $\{ V_1,V_2\}$ satisfies the generalized adjustment criterion relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[C]$.

We now consider $\g[P]$. 
To block the path $X_2 \leftarrow V_2 \leftrightarrow Y$, we must use node $V_2$. But, $V_2 \in \mathrm{De}(X_1,\g[P])$ and thus there is no set satisfying the generalized back-door criterion relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[P]$. However, sets $\{ V_1,V_2\}$, $\{V_1,V_2,V_3\}$, $\{V_1,V_2,V_4\}$, $\{V_1,V_2,V_3,V_4\}$ all satisfy the generalized adjustment criterion relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[P]$.
nodes.statement_short: For multiple treatments in a CPDAG and a PAG, no set satisfies the generalized back-door criterion but some sets satisfy the GAC.
nodes.label: ex4

nodes.name: Generalized back-door criterion
nodes.statement: Recall that a set $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies the generalized back-door criterion relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ and a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ if $\mathbf{Z}$ contains no possible descendants of $\mathbf{X}$ in $\g$ and if for every $X \in \mathbf{X}$ the set $\mathbf{Z}\cup \mathbf{X}\setminus\{X\}$ blocks every definite status path from $X$ to every $Y \in \mathbf{Y}$ in $\g$ that does not start with a visible edge out of $X$.
nodes.statement_short: Z satisfies the generalized back-door criterion if it has no possible descendants of X and, with the other X's, blocks every definite status path not starting with a visible edge out of X.

nodes.name: Adjustment Criterion (AC)
nodes.origin_citation: Shpitser et al. 2010; van der Zander et al. 2014
nodes.statement_short: For DAGs and MAGs: amenability, no Z-node descends from a non-X node on a proper causal path, and Z blocks all proper non-causal paths.
nodes.label: defac

nodes.name: AC is a reformulation of earlier criteria
nodes.statement: This adjustment criterion is a slightly reformulated but equivalent version of the adjustment criterion of \citet{shpitser2012validity} for $\mathrm{DAG}$s and of \citet{vanconstructing} for $\mathrm{MAG}$s, with amenability directly included in the criterion.

nodes.name: Soundness and completeness of the adjustment criterion for DAGs and MAGs
nodes.statement: This adjustment criterion was shown to be sound and complete for $\mathrm{DAG}$s \citep{shpitser2012validity,shpitser2012avalidity} and $\mathrm{MAG}$s \citep{vanconstructing}.
nodes.origin_citation: Shpitser et al. 2010; van der Zander et al. 2014
conclusions: This adjustment criterion was shown to be sound and complete for $\mathrm{DAG}$s \citep{shpitser2012validity,shpitser2012avalidity} and $\mathrm{MAG}$s \citep{vanconstructing}

nodes.name: Reduction of Theorem 3.4 to CPDAGs and PAGs
nodes.statement: We therefore only need to prove Theorem \ref{thmgenac} for $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s and $\mathrm{PAG}$s.
nodes.statement_short: Since the AC is sound and complete for DAGs and MAGs, the theorem only needs proof for CPDAGs and PAGs.

nodes.name: Setting for Section 5: CPDAG or PAG with disjoint X, Y, Z
nodes.statement: Throughout, we let $\mathcal G=(\vars, \e)$ represent a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ or a $\mathrm{PAG}$, and we let $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ be pairwise disjoint subsets of $\vars$, with $\mathbf{X}\neq \emptyset$ and $\mathbf{Y}\neq \emptyset$.

nodes.name: Abbreviations GAC and AC
nodes.statement: We use GAC and AC to refer to the generalized adjustment criterion (Definition \ref{defacgen}) and adjustment criterion (Definition \ref{defac}), respectively.

nodes.name: Amenability lemma (condition (0))
nodes.statement: If a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ satisfies condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$, then every $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$ satisfies condition (0*) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. On the other hand, if $\g$ violates condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$, then there exists no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (see Definition \ref{defadjustment}).
assumptions: a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ satisfies condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$
$\g$ violates condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$
conclusions: every $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$ satisfies condition (0*) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$
there exists no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (see Definition \ref{defadjustment})

assumptions: a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ satisfies condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$
conclusions: every $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$ satisfies condition (0*) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$

assumptions: $\g$ violates condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$
conclusions: there exists no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X}\cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$ (see Definition \ref{defadjustment})

nodes.statement_short: If a CPDAG/PAG is amenable, every DAG/MAG in its class is amenable; if not, no adjustment set exists.
nodes.label: lemmaadjamengen

nodes.name: Equivalence of condition (1) of the GAC and condition (a) of the AC
assumptions: Let condition (0) of the GAC be satisfied relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$.
conclusions: the following two statements are equivalent
equivalent_conditions: $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies condition (1) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
$\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies condition (a) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in every $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$.
nodes.statement_short: For an amenable CPDAG/PAG, Z satisfies GAC condition (1) iff it satisfies AC condition (a) in every represented DAG/MAG.
nodes.label: lemmaprovingeqofacconditiona

nodes.name: Equivalence of condition (2) of the GAC and condition (b) of the AC
assumptions: Let condition (0) of the GAC be satisfied relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$
let $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfy condition (1) of the GAC relative to  $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$
conclusions: the following two statements are equivalent
equivalent_conditions: $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies condition (2) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
$\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies condition (b) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in every $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$.
nodes.statement_short: For an amenable CPDAG/PAG and Z meeting condition (1), Z satisfies GAC condition (2) iff it satisfies AC condition (b) in every represented DAG/MAG.
nodes.label: lemmaequivalenceofcondb

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.4
nodes.statement:
First, suppose that the $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ and the sets $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfy all conditions of the GAC. By applying Lemmas \ref{lemmaadjamengen}, \ref{lemmaprovingeqofacconditiona} and \ref{lemmaequivalenceofcondb} in turn, it directly follows that all conditions of the AC are satisfied by $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ and any $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$.

   To prove the other direction, suppose that the tuple $\g$, $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ does not satisfy all conditions of the GAC. First, suppose that $\g$ violates condition (0) relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. Then by Lemma \ref{lemmaadjamengen}, there is no adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$, and hence $\mathbf{Z}$ is certainly not an adjustment set.

   Otherwise, $\mathbf{Z}$ must violate condition (1) or (2) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. By applying Lemmas \ref{lemmaprovingeqofacconditiona} and \ref{lemmaequivalenceofcondb} in turn, this implies that there is a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$) in $[\g]$ such that $\mathbf{Z}$ violates conditions (a) or (b) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$).
   Since the AC is sound and complete for $\mathrm{DAG}$s and $\mathrm{MAG}$s, this implies that $\mathbf{Z}$ is not an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$), so that $\mathbf{Z}$ is certainly not an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemmas 5.2-5.4 in each direction; for the converse, a violated GAC condition yields a represented DAG/MAG where the AC fails, which is not an adjustment set by soundness and completeness of the AC.

nodes.name: Directed path with invisible first edge in some MAG
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be nodes in a $\mathrm{PAG}$ $\g[P]$, such that there is a possibly directed path $\pstar$ from $X$ to $Y$ in $\g[P]$ that does not start with a visible edge out of $X$. Then there is a $\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$ in $[\g[P]]$ such that the path $p$ in $\g[M]$, consisting of the same sequence of nodes as $\pstar$ in $\g[P]$, contains a subsequence that is a directed path from $X$ to $Y$ starting with an invisible edge in $\g[M]$.
assumptions: Let $X$ and $Y$ be nodes in a $\mathrm{PAG}$ $\g[P]$, such that there is a possibly directed path $\pstar$ from $X$ to $Y$ in $\g[P]$ that does not start with a visible edge out of $X$.
conclusions: there is a $\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$ in $[\g[P]]$ such that the path $p$ in $\g[M]$, consisting of the same sequence of nodes as $\pstar$ in $\g[P]$, contains a subsequence that is a directed path from $X$ to $Y$ starting with an invisible edge in $\g[M]$
nodes.statement_short: A possibly directed PAG path not starting with a visible edge becomes, in some MAG of the class, a directed path starting with an invisible edge.
nodes.label: lemmadirectedpath

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.2
nodes.statement:
First suppose that $\g$ satisfies condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$, meaning that every proper possibly directed path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ in $\g$ starts with a visible edge out of $\mathbf{X}$. Any visible edge in $\g$ is visible in all $\mathrm{DAG}$s ($\mathrm{MAG}$s) in $[\g]$, and any proper directed path in a $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$ corresponds to a proper possibly directed path in $\g$. Hence, any proper directed path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ in any $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$ starts with a visible edge out of $\mathbf{X}$. This shows that all $\mathrm{DAG}$s ($\mathrm{MAG}$s) in $[\g]$ satisfy condition (0*) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$.

   Next, suppose that $\g$ violates condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. We will show that this implies that there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq  \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
   We give separate proofs for $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s and $\mathrm{PAG}$s.

   Thus, let $\g$ represent a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ and suppose that there is a proper possibly directed path $p$ from a node $X \in \mathbf{X}$ to a node $Y \in \mathbf{Y}$ that starts with a non-directed edge ($\setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture}$).

   Let $p' = \langle X, V_1,\dots, Y \rangle$ (where $V_1 = Y$ is allowed) be a shortest subsequence of $p$ such that $p'$ is also a proper possibly directed path from $X$ to $Y$ starting with a non-directed edge in $\g$. We first show that $p'$ is a definite status path, by contradiction. Thus, suppose that $p'$ is not a definite status path. Then the length of $p'$ is at least 2, and we write $p' = \langle X,V_1,\dots,V_k=Y\rangle$ for $k\ge 2$. Since the subpath $p'(V_1,Y)$ is a definite status path (otherwise we can choose a shorter path), this means that $V_1$ is not of a definite status on $p'$. This implies the existence of an edge between $X$ and $V_2$. This edge must be of the form $X \to V_2$, since $X \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture} V_2$ implies that we can choose a shorter path, and $X \leftarrow V_2$ together with $X \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture} V_1$ implies $V_1 \leftarrow V_2$  by Lemma 1 from \citet{meek1995causal} (see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement), so that $p'$ is not possibly directed from $X$ to $Y$. But the edge $X \to V_2$ implies that $V_1 \to V_2$, since otherwise Lemma 1 from \citet{meek1995causal} implies $X \to V_1$. But then $V_1$ is a definite non-collider on $p'$, which contradicts that $V_1$ is not of definite status.

   Hence, $p'$ is a proper possibly directed definite status path from $X$ to $Y$. By Lemma 7.6 from \citet{maathuis2013generalized} (see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement), there is a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]_1$ in $[\g]$ such that there are no additional arrowheads into $X$, as well as a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]_2$ in $[\g]$ such that there are no additional arrowheads into $V_1$. This means that the paths corresponding to $p'$ are oriented as $p'_1 = X \to V_1 \to \dots \to Y$ and $p'_2 = X \leftarrow V_1 \to \dots \to Y$ in $\g[D]_1$ and $\g[D]_2$.
   An adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]_2$ must block the non-causal path $p'_{2}$, by using at least one of the non-endpoints nodes on this path. But all these nodes are in $\fb{\g[D]_1}$ (see \eqref{eq: def forbidden nodes}). Hence, there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that satisfies the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]_1$ and $\g[D]_2$ simultaneously. Since the AC is sound and complete for $\mathrm{DAG}$s, this implies that there is no $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.

   Finally, let $\g$ represent a $\mathrm{PAG}$ and suppose that there is a proper possibly directed path $p$ from some $X\ \in \mathbf{X}$ to some $Y\in \mathbf{Y}$ that does not start with a visible edge out of $X$ in $\g$.

  By Lemma \ref{lemmadirectedpath}, there is a subsequence $p'$ of $p$ such that there is a $\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$ in $[\g]$ where the corresponding path is directed from $X$ to $Y$ and starts with an invisible edge.
   Then $\g[M]$ is not amenable relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. By Lemma 5.7 from \citet{vanconstructing} (see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement) this means that there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[M]$. Hence, there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
nodes.statement_short: Visible edges and possibly directed paths transfer to every represented graph; if amenability fails, build two represented DAGs (CPDAG case) or an invisible-edge MAG (PAG case, Lemma 5.5) admitting no common adjustment set. The CPDAG case shows a shortest such path is of definite status and orients it two ways via Lemma 7.6 of Maathuis & Colombo.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement:
First, suppose that $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies condition (1) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$. Then $\mathbf{Z} \cap \fb{\g} = \emptyset$.
   Since $\fb{\g[D]} \subseteq \fb{\g}$ ($\fb{\g[M]} \subseteq \fb{\g}$) for any $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$) in $[\g]$, it follows directly that $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfies condition (a) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in all $\mathrm{DAG}$s ($\mathrm{MAG}$s) in $[\g]$.

   To prove the other direction, suppose that $\g$ satisfies condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$, but that $\mathbf{Z}$ does not satisfy condition (1) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X,Y})$ in $\g$. Then there is a node $V \in \mathbf{Z} \cap \fb{\g}$, i.e., $V\in \mathbf{Z}$ and $V$ is a possible descendant of a node $W$ on a proper possibly directed path from some $X\in \mathbf{X}$ to some $Y\in \mathbf{Y}$ in $\g$. We denote this path by $p = \langle X, V_1,\dots, V_k, Y \rangle$, where $k\ge 1$ and $W\in \{V_1,\dots,V_k\}$. Then the subpaths $q=p(X,W)$ and $r=p(W,Y)$ are also proper possibly directed paths. Moreover, there is a possibly directed path $s$ from $W$ to $V$, where this path is allowed to be of zero length (if $W=V$). We will show that the existence of these paths implies that there is a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$) in $[\g]$ such that $\mathbf{Z}$ violates condition (a) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$).

   By Lemma B.1 from \citet{zhang2008completeness} (see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement), there are subsequences $q'$, $r'$ and $s'$ of $q$, $r$ and $s$ that are unshielded proper possibly directed paths (again $s'$ is allowed to be a path of zero length). Moreover, $q'$ must start with a directed (visible) edge, since otherwise the concatenated path $q' \oplus r'$, which is again a proper possibly directed path from $X$ to $Y$, would violate condition (0) of the GAC.

 Lemma B.1 from \citet{zhang2008completeness} then implies that $q'$ is a directed path from $X$ to $W$ in $\g$. Hence, the path corresponding to $q'$ is a directed path from $X$ to $W$ in any $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$.

   By Lemma 7.6 from \citet{maathuis2013generalized}, there is at least one $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$) in  $[\g]$ that has no additional arrowheads into $W$. In this graph $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$), the path corresponding to $r'$ is a directed path from $W$ to $Y$, and the path corresponding to $s'$ is a directed path $W$ to $V$.
   Hence,  $V \in \fb{\g[D]}$  ($V \in \fb{\g[M]}$), so that $\mathbf{Z}$ does not satisfy condition (a) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$).
nodes.statement_short: Forbidden sets of represented graphs lie in the CPDAG/PAG forbidden set; conversely, unshielded subpaths and a represented graph with no extra arrowheads into W put the offending node in a DAG/MAG forbidden set.

nodes.name: Distance-from-Z
nodes.statement: (\textbf{Distance-from-$\mathbf{Z}$}; \citealp{zhang2006causal}) Given a path $p$ from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ that is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in a $\mathrm{DAG}$ or $\mathrm{MAG}$, for every collider $Q$ on $p$, there is a directed path (possibly of zero length) from $Q$ to a member of $\mathbf{Z}$. Define the $distance-from-\!{\mathbf{Z}}$ of $Q$ to be the length of a shortest directed path (possibly of length 0) from $Q$ to $\mathbf{Z}$, and define the $distance-from-\!{\mathbf{Z}}$ of $p$ to be the sum of the distances from $\mathbf{Z}$ of the colliders on $p$.
nodes.statement_short: Distance-from-Z of a collider is its shortest directed path length to Z; of an m-connecting path, the sum over its colliders.
nodes.label: defdistancefromC

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.4
nodes.statement:
Let $\g$ represent an amenable $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) that satisfies condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$, and let $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfy condition (1) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.

   We first prove that if $\mathbf{Z}$ does not satisfy condition (2) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$, then $\mathbf{Z}$ does not satisfy condition (b) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in any $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$.
   Thus, assume that there is a proper definite status non-causal path $p$ from $X \in \mathbf{X}$ to $Y \in \mathbf{Y}$ that is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g$. Consider any $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$) in $[\g]$. Then the path corresponding to $p$ in $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$) is a proper non-causal m-connecting path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ given $\mathbf{Z}$. Hence,
   $\mathbf{Z}$ violates condition (b) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ and $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$).

   Next, we prove that if $\mathbf{Z}$ violates condition (b) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in some $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$, then $\mathbf{Z}$ violates condition (2) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
   Thus, assume that there is a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$) in $[\g]$ such that there is a proper non-causal m-connecting path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ in $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$) given $\mathbf{Z}$.
   We choose a shortest such path $p$, such that no equally short proper non-causal m-connecting path has a shorter $distance-from-\!{\mathbf{Z}}$ than $p$. By Lemma \ref{lemma22} below, the corresponding path $\pstar$ in $\g$ is an m-connecting proper definite status non-causal path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ given $\mathbf{Z}$. Hence $\mathbf{Z}$ violates condition (b) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.

nodes.name: Shortest m-connecting non-causal path is of definite status in the PAG
nodes.statement: Let $\g[M]$ represent a $\mathrm{MAG}$ ($\mathrm{DAG}$) and let $\g[P]$ be the $\mathrm{PAG}$ ($\mathrm{CPDAG}$) of $\g[M]$. Let $\g[P]$ satisfy condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$,  and let $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfy condition (1) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[P]$. Let $p$ be a shortest proper non-causal path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ that is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[M]$ and let $\pstar$ denote the corresponding path constituted by the same sequence of variables in $\g[P]$. Then $\pstar$ is a proper definite status non-causal path in $\g[P]$.
assumptions: Let $\g[M]$ represent a $\mathrm{MAG}$ ($\mathrm{DAG}$) and let $\g[P]$ be the $\mathrm{PAG}$ ($\mathrm{CPDAG}$) of $\g[M]$.
Let $\g[P]$ satisfy condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$,
let $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfy condition (1) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[P]$.

Let $p$ be a shortest proper non-causal path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ that is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[M]$ and let $\pstar$ denote the corresponding path constituted by the same sequence of variables in $\g[P]$.
conclusions: $\pstar$ is a proper definite status non-causal path in $\g[P]$
nodes.statement_short: A shortest proper non-causal m-connecting path in a MAG (DAG) corresponds to a proper definite status non-causal path in its PAG (CPDAG).
nodes.label: lemma11

nodes.name: Shortest minimal-distance m-connecting path stays m-connecting in the PAG
nodes.statement: Let $\g[M]$ represent a $\mathrm{MAG}$ ($\mathrm{DAG}$) and let $\g[P]$ be the $\mathrm{PAG}$ ($\mathrm{CPDAG}$) of $\g[M]$. Let $\g[P]$ satisfy condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$, and let $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfy condition (1) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[P]$. Let $p$ be a shortest proper non-causal path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ that is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[M]$, such that no equally short such path has a shorter $distance-from-\!{\mathbf{Z}}$ than $p$. Let $\pstar$ denote the corresponding path constituted by the same sequence of variables in $\g[P]$. Then $\pstar$ is a proper definite status non-causal path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ that is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[P]$.

Let $\g[P]$ satisfy condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$,
let $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfy condition (1) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[P]$.

Let $\pstar$ denote the corresponding path constituted by the same sequence of variables in $\g[P]$.

nodes.label: lemma22

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.8
nodes.statement:
By Lemma \ref{lemma11}, $\pstar$ is a proper definite status non-causal path in $\g[P]$. It is only left to prove that $\pstar$ is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[P]$.
   
Every definite non-collider on $\pstar$ in $\g[P]$ corresponds to a non-collider on $p$ in $\g[M]$, and every collider on $\pstar$ is also a collider on $p$. Since $p$ is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$, no non-collider is in $\mathbf{Z}$ and every collider has a descendant in $\mathbf{Z}$. Let $Q$ be an arbitrary collider (if there is one). Then there is a directed path (possibly of zero length) from $Q$ to a node in $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[M]$. Let $d$ be a shortest such path from $Q$ to a node $Z \in \mathbf{Z}$. Let $\pstar[d]$ denote the corresponding path in $\g[P]$, constituted by the same sequence of variables. Then $\pstar[d]$ is an unshielded possibly directed path from $Q$ to $Z$ in $\g[P]$ (Lemma B.1 from \citet{zhang2008completeness}).
   
   It is only left to show that $\pstar[d]$ is a directed path. If $\pstar[d]$ is of zero length, this is trivially true. Otherwise,
  suppose for contradiction that there is a circle mark on $\pstar[d]$. Then $\pstar[d]$ must start with a circle mark at $Q$ 
  (cf.\ Lemma B.2 from \citealp{zhang2008completeness} and Lemma 7.2 from \citealp{maathuis2013generalized}; see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement).
  
 Let $S$ be the first node on $d$ after $Q$.
 If $S$ is not a node on $p$, then following the proof of Lemma 2 from \citet{zhang2006causal} there is a path  $p' = p(X,W) \oplus W \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(0.2,0){$\bullet$} \put(1,0){$\rightarrow$} \end{picture} S \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(0.2,0){$\leftarrow$} \put(3,0){$\bullet$} \end{picture} V \oplus p(V,Y)$, where $W$ and $V$ are nodes distinct from $Q$ on $p(X,Q)$ and $p(Q,Y)$ respectively and $p'$ is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[M]$.
 Since $p'$ is non-causal and shorter than $p$, or as long as $p$ but with a shorter $distance-from-\!{\mathbf{Z}}$ than $p$, the path $p'$ must be non-proper, i.e. $S \in \mathbf{X}$.  But, in that case the path $\langle S,V \rangle \oplus p(V,Y)$ is a proper non-causal m-connecting path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ given $\mathbf{Z}$ that is shorter than $p$ in $\g[M]$. This contradicts our assumption about $p$.

 If $S$ is a node on $p$, then it lies either on $p(X,Q)$ or $p(Q,Y)$. Assume without loss of generality that $S$ is on $p(Q,Y)$. Following the proof of Lemma 2 from \citet{zhang2006causal}, there exists a path $p' =p(X,W) \oplus  W  \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(0.2,0){$\bullet$} \put(1,0){$\rightarrow$} \end{picture} S  \oplus p(S,Y)$ in $\g[M]$, where $W$ is a node on $p(X,Q)$ distinct from $Q$ that is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[M]$.
Since $p'$  is proper, and shorter than $p$, or as long as $p$ but with a shorter $distance-from-\!{\mathbf{Z}}$ than $p$, the path $p'$ must be causal in $\g[M]$. Let $\pstar[p']$ denote the corresponding path constituted by the same sequence of variables in $\g[P]$.  Then $\pstar[p']$ is a possibly causal path and $Z \in \mathrm{PossDe}(S,\g[P])$, so $Z \in \fb{\g[P]} \cap \mathbf{Z}$. This is in contradiction with our assumption of $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfying condition ($1$) of the GAC relative to ($\mathbf{X,Y}$) in $\g[P]$.

 Thus, the path $\pstar[d]$ is directed and $Q$ is an ancestor of $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[P]$. This proves that $\pstar$ is a proper definite status non-causal path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ that is m-connecting given $\mathbf{Z}$ in $\g[M]$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.7 gives definite status; colliders keep their descendants in Z because a shortest directed path to Z must be directed in the PAG, else a shorter or closer m-connecting path or a forbidden Z-node arises.

nodes.name: Constructive version of the GAC
nodes.statement:
A
logical next step for future research would be to transform
our criterion into an algorithmically constructive version that
could be used to efficiently perform tasks like enumeration
of all minimal adjustment sets for a given graph.
nodes.statement_short: Turn the GAC into an algorithmically constructive criterion enabling efficient enumeration of minimal adjustment sets.

nodes.name: Constructive adjustment results extend to CPDAGs and PAGs
nodes.statement:
This has already
been done for $\mathrm{DAG}$s and $\mathrm{MAG}$s by \citet{vanconstructing},
and we strongly suspect that their results can be extended
to $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s and $\mathrm{PAG}$s as well.
conclusions:
their results can be extended
to $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s and $\mathrm{PAG}$s as well

nodes.name: Checkable condition for existence of an adjustment set
nodes.statement:
In a similar spirit, it would be desirable to
have an easily checkable condition to determine if there exists any adjustment
set at all, as done for the generalized back-door criterion for single interventions by \citet{maathuis2013generalized}.

nodes.name: Relaxing the no-selection-variables restriction
nodes.statement:
Future work might also explore
under which circumstances our restriction
to not allow for latent selection variables might be relaxed,
or whether our criterion could be combined with methods to
recover from selection bias \citep{Bareinboim2014}.

nodes.name: Reading a DAG as a MAG gives confounding-robust adjustment sets
nodes.statement:
As pointed out in Section~\ref{sec: examples}, our criterion sometimes has to interpret
$\mathrm{PAG}$s or $\mathrm{MAG}$s differently than $\mathrm{DAG}$s or $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s.
This is the case precisely when the first edge on some proper
possibly
causal path in a $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$ is not visible.
However, this difference in interpretation
is irrelevant for $\mathrm{DAG}$s or $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s that would be
amenable when viewed as a $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$.
For instance, if we are given a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$
that is amenable when interpreted as a $\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$,
then its
adjustment sets also work for every $\mathrm{DAG}$ that the $\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$
represents, many of which could contain
latent confounding variables. Reading a $\mathrm{DAG}$ as a $\mathrm{MAG}$
(or a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ as a $\mathrm{PAG}$) can thus allow computing adjustment
sets that are to some extent invariant to confounding.
nodes.statement_short: The GAC treats MAGs/PAGs differently from DAGs/CPDAGs exactly when a first edge is invisible; reading a DAG as a MAG yields adjustment sets robust to latent confounding.

nodes.name: Adjustment sets require identifiability
nodes.statement: We note that an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in a given graph can only exist if the total causal effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is identifiable in the graph. If the effect of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ is  not identifiable, one may be interested in computing all possible total causal effects of $\mathbf{X}$ on $\mathbf{Y}$ for $\mathrm{DAG}$s represented by the given graph. Such an approach is used in the IDA algorithm of \cite{MaathuisKalischBuehlmann09,MaathuisColomboKalischBuehlmann10}, by  considering all $\mathrm{DAG}$s represented by a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ and applying back-door adjustment to each of these $\mathrm{DAG}$s. Similar ideas could be used for $\mathrm{MAG}$s and $\mathrm{PAG}$s, but listing all relevant $\mathrm{DAG}$s described by a $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$ seems rather non-trivial.
nodes.statement_short: Adjustment sets exist only for identifiable effects; otherwise one may compute all possible effects as in IDA.

nodes.name: Instruments imply amenability
nodes.statement:
There is also an interesting connection between amenability and instrumental variables:
a $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$ $\g$ with $\mathbf{X}=\{X\}$
is amenable with respect to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ whenever it
contains an \emph{instrument} $I$,
i.e.\ there exists a variable that is a parent of $X$ but not a parent
of any child of $X$ (e.g., $I$ in Figure~\ref{fig:cpdagexample}a).
assumptions: a $\mathrm{MAG}$ or $\mathrm{PAG}$ $\g$ with $\mathbf{X}=\{X\}$

it
contains an \emph{instrument} $I$
nodes.statement_short: A MAG or PAG with a single treatment X that contains an instrument (a parent of X that is not a parent of any child of X) is amenable.

nodes.name: GAC implies AC in every represented graph
nodes.statement: First, suppose that the $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ ($\mathrm{PAG}$) $\g$ and the sets $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ satisfy all conditions of the GAC. By applying Lemmas \ref{lemmaadjamengen}, \ref{lemmaprovingeqofacconditiona} and \ref{lemmaequivalenceofcondb} in turn, it directly follows that all conditions of the AC are satisfied by $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ and any $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemmas 5.2-5.4 to get the AC in every DAG/MAG of the class

nodes.name: Converse direction setup
nodes.statement: To prove the other direction, suppose that the tuple $\g$, $\mathbf{X}$, $\mathbf{Y}$, $\mathbf{Z}$ does not satisfy all conditions of the GAC.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the GAC fails

nodes.name: Case: amenability fails
nodes.statement: First, suppose that $\g$ violates condition (0) relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. Then by Lemma \ref{lemmaadjamengen}, there is no adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$, and hence $\mathbf{Z}$ is certainly not an adjustment set.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 5.2 rules out any adjustment set

nodes.name: Case: condition (1) or (2) fails
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, $\mathbf{Z}$ must violate condition (1) or (2) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. By applying Lemmas \ref{lemmaprovingeqofacconditiona} and \ref{lemmaequivalenceofcondb} in turn, this implies that there is a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$) in $[\g]$ such that $\mathbf{Z}$ violates conditions (a) or (b) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$).
   Since the AC is sound and complete for $\mathrm{DAG}$s and $\mathrm{MAG}$s, this implies that $\mathbf{Z}$ is not an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]$ ($\g[M]$), so that $\mathbf{Z}$ is certainly not an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 5.3-5.4 give a DAG/MAG violating the AC, so Z is not an adjustment set

nodes.name: Amenable case
nodes.statement: First suppose that $\g$ satisfies condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$, meaning that every proper possibly directed path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ in $\g$ starts with a visible edge out of $\mathbf{X}$. Any visible edge in $\g$ is visible in all $\mathrm{DAG}$s ($\mathrm{MAG}$s) in $[\g]$, and any proper directed path in a $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$ corresponds to a proper possibly directed path in $\g$. Hence, any proper directed path from $\mathbf{X}$ to $\mathbf{Y}$ in any $\mathrm{DAG}$ ($\mathrm{MAG}$) in $[\g]$ starts with a visible edge out of $\mathbf{X}$. This shows that all $\mathrm{DAG}$s ($\mathrm{MAG}$s) in $[\g]$ satisfy condition (0*) of the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$.
nodes.statement_short: Visibility and possibly directed paths transfer to every represented DAG/MAG

nodes.name: Non-amenable case
nodes.statement:
Next, suppose that $\g$ violates condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. We will show that this implies that there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq  \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
   We give separate proofs for $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s and $\mathrm{PAG}$s.

   Thus, let $\g$ represent a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ and suppose that there is a proper possibly directed path $p$ from a node $X \in \mathbf{X}$ to a node $Y \in \mathbf{Y}$ that starts with a non-directed edge ($\setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture}$).

   Let $p' = \langle X, V_1,\dots, Y \rangle$ (where $V_1 = Y$ is allowed) be a shortest subsequence of $p$ such that $p'$ is also a proper possibly directed path from $X$ to $Y$ starting with a non-directed edge in $\g$. We first show that $p'$ is a definite status path, by contradiction. Thus, suppose that $p'$ is not a definite status path. Then the length of $p'$ is at least 2, and we write $p' = \langle X,V_1,\dots,V_k=Y\rangle$ for $k\ge 2$. Since the subpath $p'(V_1,Y)$ is a definite status path (otherwise we can choose a shorter path), this means that $V_1$ is not of a definite status on $p'$. This implies the existence of an edge between $X$ and $V_2$. This edge must be of the form $X \to V_2$, since $X \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture} V_2$ implies that we can choose a shorter path, and $X \leftarrow V_2$ together with $X \setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture} V_1$ implies $V_1 \leftarrow V_2$  by Lemma 1 from \citet{meek1995causal} (see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement), so that $p'$ is not possibly directed from $X$ to $Y$. But the edge $X \to V_2$ implies that $V_1 \to V_2$, since otherwise Lemma 1 from \citet{meek1995causal} implies $X \to V_1$. But then $V_1$ is a definite non-collider on $p'$, which contradicts that $V_1$ is not of definite status.

   Hence, $p'$ is a proper possibly directed definite status path from $X$ to $Y$. By Lemma 7.6 from \citet{maathuis2013generalized} (see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement), there is a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]_1$ in $[\g]$ such that there are no additional arrowheads into $X$, as well as a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]_2$ in $[\g]$ such that there are no additional arrowheads into $V_1$. This means that the paths corresponding to $p'$ are oriented as $p'_1 = X \to V_1 \to \dots \to Y$ and $p'_2 = X \leftarrow V_1 \to \dots \to Y$ in $\g[D]_1$ and $\g[D]_2$.
   An adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]_2$ must block the non-causal path $p'_{2}$, by using at least one of the non-endpoints nodes on this path. But all these nodes are in $\fb{\g[D]_1}$ (see \eqref{eq: def forbidden nodes}). Hence, there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that satisfies the AC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[D]_1$ and $\g[D]_2$ simultaneously. Since the AC is sound and complete for $\mathrm{DAG}$s, this implies that there is no $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.

   Finally, let $\g$ represent a $\mathrm{PAG}$ and suppose that there is a proper possibly directed path $p$ from some $X\ \in \mathbf{X}$ to some $Y\in \mathbf{Y}$ that does not start with a visible edge out of $X$ in $\g$.

  By Lemma \ref{lemmadirectedpath}, there is a subsequence $p'$ of $p$ such that there is a $\mathrm{MAG}$ $\g[M]$ in $[\g]$ where the corresponding path is directed from $X$ to $Y$ and starts with an invisible edge.
   Then $\g[M]$ is not amenable relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. By Lemma 5.7 from \citet{vanconstructing} (see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement) this means that there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g[M]$. Hence, there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
nodes.statement_short: Show no adjustment set exists, separately for CPDAGs and PAGs

nodes.name: Goal and split into graph classes
nodes.statement:
Next, suppose that $\g$ violates condition (0) of the GAC relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$. We will show that this implies that there is no set $\mathbf{Z}' \subseteq  \vars \setminus (\mathbf{X} \cup \mathbf{Y})$ that is an adjustment set relative to $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$ in $\g$.
   We give separate proofs for $\mathrm{CPDAG}$s and $\mathrm{PAG}$s.
nodes.statement_short: State the goal and split into CPDAG and PAG cases

nodes.name: CPDAG case
nodes.statement:
Thus, let $\g$ represent a $\mathrm{CPDAG}$ and suppose that there is a proper possibly directed path $p$ from a node $X \in \mathbf{X}$ to a node $Y \in \mathbf{Y}$ that starts with a non-directed edge ($\setlength{\unitlength}{1mm} \begin{picture}(5,1)(0,0) \put(1,1){\circle{1}} \put(1.5,1){\line(1,0){2}} \put(4,1){\circle{1}} \end{picture}$).

   Hence, $p'$ is a proper possibly directed definite status path from $X$ to $Y$. By Lemma 7.6 from \citet{maathuis2013generalized} (see Section \ref{S-sec:1} of the supplement), there is a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]_1$ in $[\g]$ such that there are no additional arrowheads into $X$, as well as a $\mathrm{DAG}$ $\g[D]_2$ in $[\g]$ such that there are no additional arrowheads into $V_1$. But all these nodes are in $\fb{\g[D]_1}$ (see \eqref{eq: def forbidden nodes}).
